opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing I think about most is how many of the smartest people I know ended up optimizing ad click-through rates or building slightly better trading strategies. I don't want to be preachy about it, because those are hard problems and people should do what they find interesting. But when you look at where the marginal brilliant person goes, the incentives are lopsided toward things that are legible and pay off quickly.

What I'd love to see is more of that talent flowing into the physical sciences, especially biology and chemistry, where machine learning is starting to change what's possible. For a long time, if you were a strong ML person, going into biology meant a pay cut, slower feedback loops, and working with messy data in a field whose culture and vocabulary were completely foreign. A lot of people bounced off for very rational reasons.

That's changing. The tools have gotten good enough that a computational person can make a real dent in things like protein design or drug discovery. You can actually design something, test it, and see it work. That loop is incredibly motivating once you've felt it. The bottleneck now is less about whether the problems are tractable and more about whether we can get enough people who can sit on both sides, who understand the models and the wet lab well enough to ask the right questions.

So concretely, I'd want more bridges. Fellowships, companies, and academic programs that make it easy for an ML engineer to spend a year really learning the biology without derailing their career. And on the other side, giving biologists real fluency with these tools, so it's not just a handoff where one group throws data over the wall to the other.

The other piece is patience in capital. A lot of the most important problems in science don't fit a two-year return horizon. If we can build funding structures, whether that's philanthropy, focused research organizations, or more patient venture, that let talented people work on ten-year problems without feeling like they're sacrificing everything, I think you'd see a big shift. People want to work on things that matter. We just have to stop making it so expensive for them to do it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions pay cuts, slow feedback, and unfamiliar biology culture and vocabulary as deterrents, but does not identify a perceived need for formal academic credentials.

r002.rationale: It says biology’s culture and vocabulary can feel foreign, but does not clearly identify biology’s conceptual obscurity as a barrier.

r003.rationale: It says the tools let a computational person make a real dent in protein design or drug discovery, communicating that computational contributors can help without first being biology specialists.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest misallocation right now is how many of the smartest people I know are working on problems where the marginal value of one more brilliant person is close to zero. You've got incredibly talented ML researchers optimizing ad click-through by a tenth of a percent, or building the fifteenth variant of a chat assistant, when the hard, high-leverage problems in biology, materials, and the physical sciences are starved for exactly that kind of talent.

Part of it is structural. If you're a strong engineer coming out of school, the path of least resistance is a big tech company or a well-funded foundation model lab. The compensation is obvious, the tooling is mature, and the problems are legible. Biology is the opposite. The data is messy, the feedback loops are slow, the experiments cost real money and real time, and you have to learn a whole second discipline just to understand what question you're even asking. So people rationally avoid it, even though that's precisely where the frontier is widest open.

What I'd like to see is more people treating that friction as the opportunity rather than the deterrent. The places where machine learning hasn't been applied well yet aren't unexplored because they're uninteresting. They're unexplored because they're hard, and because the people who understand the domain and the people who understand the models rarely sit in the same room. When you do get those people together, the progress is disproportionate. Protein design is a good example. Five years ago it was a niche. Now you can generate functional binders in silico with a hit rate that would have sounded like science fiction. That didn't happen because of more compute alone. It happened because a relatively small number of people decided to live in both worlds.

So concretely: I'd love to see a lot more of the early-career talent going into applied science domains, and I'd love to see the incentives change to make that less of a sacrifice. Better compensation for research engineering in biotech, more funding for the unglamorous infrastructure work of building datasets and experimental pipelines, and frankly more status attached to solving a real problem versus publishing another benchmark result. If even ten percent of the people currently working on general-purpose models redirected toward drug discovery or climate or energy, I think the impact over the next decade would be enormous.

r001.rationale: The response describes biology’s difficult data, slow feedback, and need to learn another discipline, but does not mention formal academic credentials as a deterrent.

r002.rationale: It says biology requires learning a whole second discipline just to understand what question to ask, presenting that conceptual difficulty as part of why talent avoids the field.

r003.rationale: The response says domain experts and model experts rarely work together, but does not state that someone can contribute computationally without a highly specialized biology background.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see more talented people working on problems where progress would make a meaningful difference in people’s lives. There are a lot of smart people optimizing things at the margin, and I’d love for more of them to have a viable path into science, medicine, energy—areas where there’s still so much we don’t know how to do.

But I think that’s mostly an incentives question. It’s easy to say, “Go work on something important.” It’s harder if that means taking a huge financial risk, spending years getting credentials, or fighting for funding. So I’d want to make those paths more accessible: give people room to learn, resources to experiment, and enough stability to stick with a hard problem.

r001.rationale: The response mentions years spent getting credentials as a general barrier to important work, but does not identify biology as the field deterred.

r002.rationale: It does not describe biology as conceptually obscure or identify that as a barrier to attracting talent.

r003.rationale: It does not state that people can contribute computationally to biology without a specialized biology background.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see more talented people working on problems where success would make a real difference to people’s lives. There are strong incentives to go into finance, advertising, or incremental software businesses, and fewer clear paths into areas like scientific research, energy, and healthcare.

I don’t think the answer is to tell people where they should work. It’s to make those other paths more attractive: give people resources, autonomy, and room to take risks. If someone wants to tackle a hard problem, getting started shouldn’t depend on already knowing the right people or being able to go without a salary.

r001.rationale: It mentions barriers to entering fields generally, but does not identify academic credentials as a deterrent to entering biology.

r002.rationale: It does not describe biology’s conceptual obscurity or identify it as a barrier to attracting talent.

r003.rationale: It does not say that people can contribute computationally to biology without specialized biology training.
